episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, June twenty-sixth, twenty-twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.

<break time="1.0s"/>

The top story this week comes from the intersection of federal policy and frontier A.I. development. According to reporting from CNN and Tech Policy Press, the U.S. government has granted limited access to Anthropic's most powerful A.I. model, following a two-week restriction that began June twelfth. The Commerce Department issued a letter confirming that a select group of trusted U.S. organizations may now use the model, partially reversing an export-control directive triggered by a reported security vulnerability in Anthropic's public-facing system. Anthropic characterized that vulnerability as a small number of previously known, minor issues. White House adviser David Sacks disagreed sharply, saying it was, quote, difficult to fathom how a jailbreak allowing operability of a cyber weapon could be defined as not serious. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, in lifting the restriction, wrote that Anthropic had made progress and that appropriate safeguards are now in place. A third perspective came from independent security researchers, including Luta Security CEO Katie Moussouris, and more than one hundred experts who signed an open letter arguing that the restriction removed a tool defenders rely on without meaningfully reducing risk. The letter called for any future A.I. restrictions to be enforced transparently and fairly. For university researchers, the episode shows that access to frontier A.I. models is increasingly shaped by federal policy decisions.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Case Study coverage this week, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reports on how composition faculty turned A.I. hallucinations into a teaching tool. Daniel Anderson, director of the UNC Writing Program and professor of English and comparative literature, allowed students to use generative A.I. throughout a course and found it useful for brainstorming and summarizing verified documents. But in literature reviews, the technology generated false references. Those errors became structured lessons in verification. Anderson subsequently built training modules as part of the Carolina A.I. Literacy initiative, funded by the UNC School of Data Science and Society, with the goal of making all Carolina students A.I. literate. Anderson said not all students need a deep understanding of A.I., but added that knowing it is trained on data, and that data can come with limitations, is useful.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Case Study, Smithsonian Magazine profiles Casey Cuny, the twenty-twenty-four California Teacher of the Year, who teaches tenth grade honors English and senior mythology at Valencia High School in Santa Clarita. Cuny developed multi-page prompts that students use with generative A.I. tools to receive instruction tailored to their personal interests, with the A.I. applying the Socratic method to guide thinking. He also built his own A.I.-powered exit-ticket application that generates mixed-ability groupings and surfaces common misconceptions in real time. One student who had earned mostly C's and D's converted course materials into a podcast using an A.I. tool and earned straight A's for the first time. Cuny describes effective A.I. use as requiring creativity, precise vocabulary, and iterative thinking, with the human always serving as decision-maker and evaluator.

<break time="1.0s"/>

From the research front, MIT Sloan reports on a study from the MIT Center for Information Systems Research identifying what separates organizations that succeed with A.I. from those that do not. The key factor, according to researchers, is data liquidity, defined as the ease with which data assets can be reused and recombined. A study of Caterpillar's multiyear data transformation identified three practical levers: data architecture, data preparation, and data permissioning. Caterpillar built a modular platform designed for reuse, created a dedicated data quality group using algorithmic and machine learning techniques, and applied a least-privilege access model for sensitive datasets. The researchers noted that companies with high data liquidity outperform peers on customer experience and speed to market. Principal research scientist Barbara Wixom co-authored the study with Joaquin Rodriguez, Gabriele Piccoli, and Cynthia Beath.

<break time="1.0s"/>

A second research finding this week, published in Computers and Composition, examines how generative A.I. changes the writing process for undergraduates. The study, led by Abram Anders of Iowa State University and Emily Dux Speltz of Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, followed thirty-eight students from twenty-two majors over two semesters. Researchers found that A.I. does not make writing easier. It shifts the effort from transcription to higher-order thinking. Anders identified what he calls a fluency trap, in which polished A.I. output leads students to trust content that is shallow or factually wrong. The researchers identified three threshold concepts for effective A.I. writing: treating A.I. use as experimental and iterative, applying genuine subject expertise to evaluate output, and maintaining human ownership of meaning and purpose. The study design is qualitative with a small cohort.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers, a newly proposed federal bill would create tax incentives for employers that partner with public colleges on workforce training. The Supporting Knowledge Through Industry-Led Learning Act, introduced by Congressman Sam Liccardo of California, would establish five hundred million dollars annually in tax credits. Companies would receive twenty-five hundred dollars for each student completing a qualifying program and an additional twenty-five hundred dollars if they hire that graduate. ABC7 Bay Area reports the bill builds on a California collaboration launched in summer twenty-twenty-four to bring A.I.-related curriculum to community colleges statewide. NVIDIA's Louis Stewart, head of ecosystem development, said workforce pipelines need to be built before disruption occurs, not after it.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Insights and Trends, Forbes reports that between twenty-twenty-one and twenty-twenty-five, Chinese universities eliminated roughly twelve thousand two hundred undergraduate degree programs and introduced approximately ten thousand two hundred new ones, affecting more than thirty percent of undergraduate programs nationwide, according to China's Ministry of Education. Programs cut included humanities, arts, foreign languages, and some management disciplines. New programs focus on artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductor engineering, and advanced manufacturing. China now produces more than twelve million university graduates each year. Forbes contributor Anna Esaki-Smith contrasts China's government-directed approach with U.S. program cuts, which are typically driven by enrollment declines and budget pressures rather than national industrial strategy.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And in Investing in Innovation, a new national nonprofit called RAISE US has launched with a goal of raising one billion dollars for A.I. workforce retraining. EdTech Innovation Hub reports the organization has already secured more than half that target. Founded by former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo and former Indiana Governor Eric Holcomb, RAISE counts Amazon, Anthropic, Microsoft, and the OpenAI Foundation as anchor partners. Bank of America is the primary sponsor of an advanced manufacturing apprenticeship initiative. Initial state programs are underway in Arkansas, Connecticut, Maryland, and Utah, including an A.I.-powered career navigation system in Arkansas called Arkansas LAUNCH. A dedicated Policy Lab, funded separately from corporate contributions, will test worker support models including wage insurance and short-time compensation. Raimondo stated that America has a technology strategy for leading the global A.I. competition but does not yet have a people strategy, and cannot lead without one.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: Anthropic's Most Powerful AI Returns to Limited Use After a Two-Week Standoff
leadStory.summary:
Anthropic said on Friday that the U.S. government has allowed it to release its Claude Mythos 5 artificial intelligence model to some "trusted" U.S. organizations, partially reversing an order two weeks earlier to suspend access over national security risks. The U.S. government granted access to a group of select companies and organizations, according to a letter from the Commerce Department.

Anthropic markets Mythos as its strongest cybersecurity model, the same capability that made it the focus of both the company's own risk warnings and the government's restriction. Two weeks before the standoff, CEO Dario Amodei publicly called frontier models like Mythos an "emblematic example" of the national-security threat advanced AI poses, urging "mandatory testing by a qualified third party" of risks including cybersecurity and biological weapons. Yet after a June 12 export-control directive, triggered by a reported jailbreak of the safeguards on Fable 5, the company's public-facing model, Anthropic disabled both Fable 5 and Mythos for all users, characterizing the flagged vulnerability as "a small number of previously known, minor vulnerabilities."

The two sides described the same issue very differently. White House adviser David Sacks said it was "difficult to fathom how they could claim a jailbreak allowing operability of a cyber weapon could be defined as not 'serious,'" while Anthropic maintained the risk was already present in other public models. In lifting the restriction, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wrote that Anthropic had made progress addressing the risks and that "appropriate safeguards are in place."

Independent security researchers offered a third view: that the restriction may do more harm than good. Katie Moussouris, CEO of Luta Security, and an open letter signed by more than 100 experts argued that other models can also find software vulnerabilities, so restricting Mythos removes a tool defenders rely on without meaningfully reducing risk, and that the flagged behavior was ordinary defensive security work, not a malicious "jailbreak." The open letter urged that any future AI restrictions be "enforced transparently and fairly" through a democratic process, a pointed rebuke of an action the signatories said "created market uncertainty and risked America's AI leadership without any real risk to justify it."

For universities, the episode is a reminder that access to the most capable frontier models is increasingly shaped by federal policy, often leaving academic researchers outside the approved circle.
leadStory.source: CNN / Tech Policy Press / Newstex / freefable.org / Luta Security

quickHits.headline: UNC-Chapel Hill Faculty Use AI to Teach Verification Skills After Chatbot Hallucinations Become a Lesson Plan

quickHits.headline: California Teacher Builds Custom AI App to Personalize Lessons for 36 Students Simultaneously
quickHits.summary: Casey Cuny, the 2024 California Teacher of the Year, has developed a classroom approach using generative A.I. that delivers individualized instruction at a scale previously impossible, Smithsonian Magazine reported. Cuny teaches 10th grade honors English and senior mythology at Valencia High School in Santa Clarita. His method involves multi-page prompts that students drop into ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude — the A.I. then tailors examples to each student's personal interests and uses the Socratic method to guide their thinking. Cuny also built his own A.I.-powered exit-ticket app, Whitai.app, which generates mixed-ability groupings and surfaces common misconceptions in real time. One student, Klay, who had earned mostly C's and D's, used Google NotebookLM to convert course materials into a podcast — and earned straight A's for the first time. Cuny describes effective A.I. use as requiring creativity, precise vocabulary, and iterative thinking rather than technological skill, with the human always serving as the decision-maker and evaluator.

quickHits.headline: MIT Researchers Identify Three Data Practices That Separate AI Leaders from Laggards
quickHits.summary: Researchers at the MIT Center for Information Systems Research have identified data liquidity — the ease with which data assets can be reused and recombined — as the key differentiator between organizations that succeed with A.I. and those that don't, MIT Sloan reported. A study of Caterpillar's multiyear data transformation found three practical levers: data architecture, data preparation, and data permissioning. Caterpillar built a modular platform with a thin application layer designed for reuse, created a dedicated data quality group that validated records using algorithmic and machine learning techniques, and applied a least-privilege access model that controlled who could reach sensitive datasets. The researchers write that companies with high data liquidity outperform peers on customer experience, speed to market, and data-driven decision-making. Principal research scientist Barbara Wixom co-authored the study with Joaquin Rodriguez, Gabriele Piccoli, and Cynthia Beath.

quickHits.headline: Iowa State Study Finds AI Does Not Simplify Writing — It Raises the Cognitive Stakes
quickHits.summary: A classroom study of 38 undergraduates from 22 majors found that using generative A.I. does not make writing easier — it shifts the effort from transcription to higher-order thinking, per Futurity and the Iowa State news service, as reported by Let's Data Science. The study, published in Computers and Composition (Volume 81, 2026), was led by Abram Anders of Iowa State University and Emily Dux Speltz of Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Students completed structured assignments over two semesters while tracking how their composing process changed. Anders identified a 'fluency trap' in which polished A.I. output leads students to trust content that is shallow or factually wrong. The researchers identified three threshold concepts for effective A.I. writing: treating A.I. use as experimental and iterative, applying genuine subject expertise to evaluate output, and maintaining human ownership of meaning and purpose. The study design is qualitative with a small cohort.

quickHits.headline: Federal SKILL Act Would Pay Employers $5,000 Per Graduate to Build AI-Ready Workforce at Community Colleges
quickHits.summary: Congressman Sam Liccardo (D-San Jose) has proposed the Supporting Knowledge Through Industry-Led Learning Act, which would create $500 million annually in tax credits for employers that partner with public colleges on workforce training, ABC7 Bay Area reported. Under the proposal, companies would receive a $2,500 tax credit for each student who completes a qualifying program and an additional $2,500 if they hire that graduate. Liccardo pointed to West Valley College in Saratoga, where student Gabriel Huerta completed a tuition-free mechatronics program and transitioned into a career as an instrumentation and controls technician at Santa Clara Valley Water. The bill builds on a California-NVIDIA collaboration launched in summer 2024 to bring A.I.-related curriculum to community colleges statewide. NVIDIA's Louis Stewart said workforce pipelines must be built before disruption occurs: 'That's why the right workforce model starts before disruption, not after it.'

quickHits.headline: China Eliminated 12,200 University Programs in Four Years, Replacing Many with AI and Robotics Degrees
quickHits.summary: Between 2021 and 2025, Chinese universities ended or suspended 12,200 undergraduate degree programs and introduced approximately 10,200 new ones, affecting more than 30% of undergraduate programs nationwide, Forbes reported, citing Ministry of Education data from China's official state news agency Xinhua. Programs cut disproportionately included humanities, arts, foreign languages, and some management disciplines — fields viewed as 'obsolete.' New programs focus on artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductor engineering, and A.I.-driven advanced manufacturing. China now produces more than 12 million university graduates each year, and the urban unemployment rate for 16- to 24-year-olds who were not students rose to 16.9% in March. Forbes contributor Anna Esaki-Smith contrasts the Chinese approach — government-directed reallocation toward strategic industries — with U.S. program cuts, which are typically driven by enrollment declines and budget deficits rather than national industrial strategy.

quickHits.headline: RAISE US Launches with $500 Million Secured to Retrain Workers Displaced by AI
quickHits.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo and former Indiana Governor Eric Holcomb have launched RAISE US, a national nonprofit targeting $1 billion in commitments for A.I. workforce retraining programs, EdTech Innovation Hub reported. The organization has already secured more than half that target. Amazon, Anthropic, Microsoft, and the OpenAI Foundation are anchor partners; Bank of America is the primary sponsor of an advanced manufacturing apprenticeship initiative. Initial state partnerships are underway in Arkansas, Connecticut, Maryland, and Utah. In Arkansas, RAISE US is supporting an A.I.-powered career navigation system called Arkansas LAUNCH. Maryland plans include an accelerator for displaced workers pursuing entrepreneurship. A dedicated Policy Lab — funded separately from corporate contributions — will test worker support models including wage insurance and short-time compensation. Raimondo framed the initiative plainly: 'America has a technology strategy for leading the global AI competition. It does not yet have a people strategy \u2014 and we cannot lead without one.'
